There is a little perch by the booth window covered by a small roof; you stand on it so as to keep from the rain.
Uncomfortable to say the least.

lines.text: A standard Maglite three-cell torch, the anodising worn back to bare metal where a hand goes. You thumb it on against your palm and off again.
Working. Cells are good. I'm pretty sure I remembered to push in fresh ones in earlier today.

lines.text: Alkalines. I've got a good, continuous four or five hours of light on standby, but I don't want to get anywhere near an empty charge.
I'd have brought spares.
Everyone should bring spares... nobody really ever does though.

choices.text: and if it dies in there

lines.text: You'll want it on in there. It's black as anything past the foyer.
It goes off when the tape rolls.
Off? Why off? A torch makes no noise, it–

It makes a noise like a hand moving or a filament buzzing. It clicks. I mean, you cannot hold still with a torch on. You sweep it, and the sweep is on the tape, in your shoulder, in your coat, on your breath.
...right.
I work in the dark. It's part the job. It's really most of the job.
The last one? Had a head torch. Little red one, for the night vision, he said.
That is a good bit of kit yeah.
He came out the first two nights. Third night he went in at ten and I did my rounds and the gate was shut and his van was still there Thursday.
The rain gets briefly heavier and then lifts. It comes in patches, it's soothing white noise waxing and waning as the night slowly drags on.
Van was gone come Friday though. Who knows.
Who knows indeed... but why are you telling me this right before I head inside?

art.caption: Gate booth / coffee on the form

lines.text: He fills a second cup without asking how you take it and slides it across the form.
There. You look like you need it more than I do.
Thanks?

choices.text: ask what his wife makes of the coffee

art.caption: Work order under the booth glass

lines.text: A letterhead, a list, and a signature. That signature block has been photocopied so many times it barely passes for a smudge.
You don't argue with the pay though.
Four hundred, half on acceptance. That's fine. That's more than fine.
Four hundred for a night's work in a building with no power in it.
It's about double what I usually get. I saw the dispatch call come up on my job board at four and I said yes almost as soon as I saw it.
"The room as it is." "One clean minute." "If you can hear yourself on the take, you must start again."
That's fair.

choices.text: "if you can hear yourself, start again"

lines.text: W. Ellery Holdings. Same name as the building, which tells you nothing, because they bought the name with it.
No website. A landline and a post box in Croydon.
I've worked for worse and been paid slower.
Thursday, six in the morning. After that there is no building to be in, only dust and the land rights to a new development project.
So there's no coming back on Friday to pick up the ones I missed.
Five or none. Tonight is the whole job.
"The prior contractor delivered four accepted room tones. The packet was settled for four."
Settled for four. So they got paid, and they stopped. Maybe they just couldn't bare the dark? Happens all the time.

Nobody settles for 80% of work for anything. Not once, not ever, not without a phone call first.

Keys and forms. Past the door is nothing to do with me.
He turns the television down, but the sound was already off.

lines.text: Have you been in?
No.
Not allowed?
Not interested.
He says it the way people say they do not like anchovies.
Eleven years on the gate and you have never once had a look?
Not interested.
He says it exactly the same way. Same three words, same speed. It's not quite a façade.
It's a building, mate. I've got me chair here, and me 'telly. No need to go inside, they had other people for that.
There was someone before me. Few weeks back.
Yeah. Nice enough. Kept his own hours.
Did he come out?
The guard turns the form around and taps a box near the bottom.
Initial there as well. They want it twice now.
My shift ended at ten. I was home...

choices.text: you were home. finish the sentence
what did he leave in the booth

lines.text: What was he called, the last bloke?
Hang on.
He turns the book around and runs a finger up the column, past tonight, past the rain, into September.
There. Received, that one. And the box next to it is empty.
It is the same ledger you are about to sign.
Can't read his writing. Nobody can read anybody's writing anymore.
So who's on the gate after you?
Nobody. Site's condemned. They stopped paying for the night after they stopped paying for the power. Tonight is my last night on the job.
So I ring the bell at three in the morning and.
And nothing. Gate code is on your sheet.
It's a demolition, not a bank.
Light's gone in the basement stair. Which you knew by the looks of it, seeing as you brought yer torch.
And the radio. If it goes funny, do not shake it.
What happens if I shake it?
Nothing. That is why I said do not.
He laughs. He has been waiting all week to say that to somebody.

choices.text: do not shake it. say that again

lines.text: Four files on the card. Three are slated and clean: the previous recordist clearly announced the take number and room for each take. Take three is already running.
Take three.
Sixty clean seconds of bare room noise.
That's clean. That's three.
A chair. He stands up.

choices.text: there's no slate on this one

lines.text: Floor sits at fifty-eight decibels. No hum, no traffic, no weird handling.
It's a beautiful take. I would have sent it.
He was better than me. I need to make these recordings count.

choices.text: he was better than you. sit with that
what would you have done differently

lines.text: You slate everything. Room, take, date. You say it out loud after you roll the take.
You do it so that in eight months, when the file is a number, somebody knows what they're listening to.
You flip the tape over to the reverse side. Take four, unslated.
He slated the other three.
So either he stopped bothering, or he did not start this one.
One more and I'm out of here.
The file does not end. It goes on not ending for a while.
Who did you lose?
the fuck? ...say again?
It is how this goes. You lost her. You lost me. Now come in and look for her.
I haven't lost anybody.
Everybody has lost somebody.
Not m-.
You did everything you could to keep from losing her. It drove her away, didn't it?.
No! Why do you know this?! Who are you?
Thirty seconds of the room, at the same level as before.
Come closer.
Vague nothings you cannot make out.
Closer. Bring forth to me your body.
You will bring me another, and will lose them together.
Back forty seconds. The room, the chair, the man standing up.
Who did you lose.
Same words. Same level. Minus forty-one decibels, both times.
You have a feeling you're going to need to check your recordings extra carefully tonight.
The rest of the file is pure, clean ambient room sounds. Nine minutes of it. He does not speak again, and neither does anything else.
That is the best goddamned room tone I have ever heard.
The file ends. It does not end on anything.
He turns the book around. Two boxes on the line with your name in it.
Sign where it says received.
You sign the first box. The second one says returned, and it is about the width of a fingernail; it is empty all the way up the page.
Don't sign the other one. That's for when you come back out.
In one single gesture (likely the toughest amount of labour for him this evening), he slides the keys under the glass along with a radio in one hand, and takes form back with the other.
Channel two?
Aye. Check in on the hour.
Grey door, end of the yard is the service entrance. I'll be here till ten.
If the service leaf sticks, don't shoulder it. Main doors are through the front foyer, past the box office. Longer walk, same yard.
He is already looking at the television.
Double means rush, risk, or silence. Rush I understand — the building is rubble on Thursday.
Risk is a word for insurers. Silence is the one that pays double and asks you not to notice it paying.
In the booth, the guard watches a television with no sound on it.
The job sat on the board for nine minutes before I took it. For this money it should have gone in one.
Three names were above mine, crossed out. Crossed out is not declined. Declined gets an email. Crossed out gets a pen.
"As it is." Not "as found". Somebody wrote that carefully, or was corrected into it.
A room as found belongs to the finder. A room as it is belongs to the room. I am reading conveyancing law into a sound job now. Long night ahead.
Standard note for amateurs. You can always hear yourself. The skill is getting the room to stop pointing it out.
Except they did not hire an amateur, and the rate says they know they did not. So the sentence is not advice. It is a specification.
Rain, on the roof, in the pause where a second thought should go.
You dial it, because it is a landline and it is nine forty at night and you want to know.
It rings the way a phone rings in an empty office. You can hear the size of the room around the bell.
Eleven rings. No machine. No hold music. I put it away before somebody answers.
That number only ever rings out, that one.

That, apparently, is what I am for.
Gone since spring. They stopped replacing bulbs when the demolition date came through.
Bulbs don't know about demolition dates.
These ones did.
He does not smile when he says it, which is somehow worse than if he had.

Channel two stops being channel two.
And becomes what.
Loud.
He says it like a man reporting the weather. Then he turns the television up, remembers the sound is off, and turns it back down.

So he is still inside.

You lot are not normal.

Taped?
